title: You Can Donate to the Government — You Can't Direct It
hook: Private money paying for a public building sounds like a bargain for taxpayers. Under U.S. law it mostly isn't allowed, because the power to decide what government spends belongs to Congress.
key_points: The federal government has accepted patriotic gifts through an account dating to 1843 — but since 1982 those funds go exclusively to paying down the national debt.
The Miscellaneous Receipts Act requires officials who receive money to deposit it in the Treasury promptly, not spend it directly.
An agency may only accept and use donations if Congress has given it explicit statutory authority; the White House has no such authority for cash gifts.
The rule against 'augmenting appropriations' stops agencies from using outside money to do things Congress never funded.
In August 2026 the D.C. Court of Appeals held that private funding does not exempt the White House ballroom from needing congressional authorization.
The principle is the point: if officials could fund projects with private gifts, the legislature's control of the purse would be optional.
content_html: When President Trump demolished the East Wing in October 2025 and proposed a 90,000-square-foot ballroom paid for by private donors, the natural reaction was that taxpayers were off the hook. Ellen P. Aprill, a tax and nonprofit law scholar at UCLA, walks through why U.S. law is far less relaxed about that than intuition suggests.
extra_html: Uncle Sam can indeed receive gifts — an account for patriotic donations goes back to 1843 — but since 1982 that money is dedicated to reducing the national debt, not to projects. More broadly, the Miscellaneous Receipts Act tells officials who come into money to deposit it in the Treasury "as soon as practicable without deduction," and an agency may only accept and spend donations where Congress has explicitly authorized it. The White House itself has no such authority for cash or monetary equivalents. Behind these technicalities sits the doctrine against augmenting appropriations: an agency cannot use outside funds to expand beyond the mission and money Congress gave it. Aprill notes the National Park Service's authority runs to conservation and preservation of land and structures, not putting up new buildings, and that the president's authority over the executive residence still requires an accompanying appropriation. In August 2026 the D.C. Court of Appeals agreed that private funding did not exempt the ballroom from congressional authorization, observing that it knew of no prior instance of a president unilaterally demolishing substantial portions of the White House. The transferable idea: the legislature's power over spending only works if officials can't route around it with someone else's cash. (This card describes U.S. federal law specifically.)

related.title: Taxation & Public Budgets
related.hook: A government's budget is its values written in numbers — and taxation is how it raises the money to act at all. Follow the money to understand the priorities.

related.title: Who Really Controls Grant Money
related.hook: The legislature appropriates the money, but the executive writes the rules for handing it out. A proposed U.S. rule would let officials end a federal grant 'at any time, for any reason.'

related.title: What an Executive Order Can and Cannot Change
related.hook: A presidential order can tell the executive branch what to aim for. It can't skip the process an agency must follow — which is why headlines and reality often diverge.

related.title: The One-Justice Order That Freezes a Case
related.hook: Before the Supreme Court decides anything, a single justice can push pause. That's how White House ballroom construction kept going after two lower courts had ordered it stopped.

flashcards.prompt: Why can't an agency simply spend a private donation on a project it likes?
flashcards.back_html: Because spending requires a congressional appropriation. Using outside money to do unfunded things would "augment appropriations" — bypassing the legislature's control of the purse.

flashcards.prompt: What happens to 'patriotic' gifts made to the U.S. government since 1982?

choices.text: They are devoted exclusively to reducing the national debt
The president may allocate them to any executive project
They are returned to donors as tax credits

flashcards.explanation_html: The gift account dates to 1843, but Congress narrowed its use in 1982 to debt reduction — donors cannot pick a project.

flashcards.prompt: What did the D.C. Court of Appeals hold about the privately funded ballroom in August 2026?

choices.text: Private funding does not exempt the project from needing congressional authorization
Private funding removes any need for congressional involvement
Only foreign donations would have required approval

flashcards.explanation_html: The source of the money doesn't change who gets to authorize the spending — that's Congress.
